title: 3D on the web
notes: 25 seconds. This talk explains the production decisions behind a useful 3D website. We will use a product viewer as the example, but the same layers apply to interactive brand scenes and applications. The focus is on tool roles, tradeoffs and the handoff. Suggested total time: roughly eight minutes.

title: The stack, explained
notes: 45 seconds. The tools belong to different layers. Blender is the authoring workspace. GLB packages geometry, materials and supported animation for delivery. Three.js, a component or an engine loads the content and manages interaction. WebGL or WebGPU draws through the device GPU. HTML and CSS surround the canvas with readable content and accessible controls. A source file and a delivery file serve different purposes.

title: Blender: production-ready assets
notes: 50 seconds. Blender owns the source asset. First match the silhouette and proportions. Then prepare materials and name parts that the developer will select or animate. Bake unsupported complex shading into textures where needed. Export a GLB and compare it in the target browser lighting. A normal map can suggest small surface detail but cannot change a silhouette. Keep both the editable source and the approved export. The image is a supplied product reference, not a claim of an exact reconstructed model.

title: Three.js: the interaction loop
notes: 55 seconds. Consider a visitor clicking the lens. The page receives pointer input. A raycaster tests which scene object is under that pointer. The application updates the selected feature, moves the camera if needed and reveals an HTML explanation. The renderer draws the changed scene. OrbitControls handles common camera navigation and GLTFLoader loads the asset. The team writes the product-specific behavior. This is a proposed interaction example.

title: WebGL and WebGPU
notes: 45 seconds. WebGL and WebGPU are browser APIs rather than modeling tools. WebGL is the established route for interactive graphics. WebGPU supports a more modern rendering and compute model, but availability and benefits depend on the workload and device. Most teams use them through an engine. Three.js WebGPURenderer can fall back to WebGL 2, but features and custom shaders still require compatibility review. Switching APIs does not repair a heavy asset or guarantee higher speed.

title: Choosing the right tool
notes: 65 seconds. This table offers starting recommendations rather than a performance ranking. Choose model-viewer when the product page needs standard inspection. Spline suits visual scene exploration, with export constraints to check. Three.js offers detailed control but needs custom engineering. React Three Fiber is a way to author Three.js within an existing React app, not an alternative asset tool. Babylon.js or PlayCanvas merit a prototype for game-like apps or richer simulations. Match the choice to the hardest interaction and the maintainers.

title: Designing motion that can be interrupted
notes: 50 seconds. A timeline describes a planned sequence, but a visitor can drag, reverse scroll or leave midway. The motion handoff must define what happens after interruption. This example uses an open-cover clip authored in Blender and played in the browser. The table is an interaction specification, not a implemented product feature. Three.js AnimationMixer plays animation clips. Ensure essential information remains available with reduced motion.

title: Three ways to put it on a page
notes: 50 seconds. A component such as model-viewer or Spline Viewer lives inside the page and offers its own API. An iframe embeds a complete separately hosted viewer, convenient for reuse but more isolated from the host page. Direct JavaScript integration places the scene in the app and provides closer access to page state, at the cost of lifecycle and resize code. Webflow can use custom embeds. All routes need correct public asset URLs and testing on the published page.

title: Performance: diagnose the bottleneck
notes: 50 seconds. A small download can still be expensive to draw. Diagnose the stage that is slow. Network problems suggest reducing transfer size or delaying loading. CPU work includes parsing, decoding and scene updates. GPU cost grows with pixels, materials, shadows and effects. Measure on a representative phone. If aiming for 60 frames per second, each frame has roughly 16.7 milliseconds; that is a target calculation, not a performance claim about this viewer. Keep a poster fallback and HTML descriptions.

title: The handoff that prevents rework
notes: 45 seconds. The workflow is strongest when each discipline hands over something concrete. Designers specify states rather than only a screenshot. Motion designers specify clip names and interruption rules. Artists provide an approved export with named parts and scale. Developers integrate and test devices, errors and fallback behavior. Review together in the browser because the exported result may look different from the authoring application. This is a recommended workflow.

title: The recommended first release
notes: 35 seconds. A good first release has one accurate asset and a useful interaction. For a simple product page, a viewer component may be sufficient. For custom behavior, use a deliberate asset workflow and Three.js. If the team is exploring a visual concept, prototype in Spline before committing to implementation. Keep a poster fallback, readable content and basic controls. These are recommendations derived from the tools’ documented capabilities. Total suggested narration time is approximately eight and a half minutes.
